author: Jonathan Haidt
concept: Intuitions come first, strategic reasoning second (the elephant and the rider)
summary: Haidt's central model: moral and most everyday judgments are made fast and intuitively (the elephant), and conscious reasoning (the rider) mostly arrives afterward to justify the gut call, like a press secretary, not a judge. People rarely reason to a conclusion; they feel it, then build the case. This makes argument-by-evidence weak against a made-up mind.
usable_principle: Expect people (and yourself) to decide intuitively and rationalize after; to move someone, speak to the intuition first, not the logic.

author: Jonathan Haidt
concept: Moral foundations: there is more to morality than harm and fairness
summary: Haidt maps several moral foundations people draw on in different proportions: care/harm, fairness/cheating, loyalty/betrayal, authority/subversion, sanctity/degradation (and liberty/oppression). Groups and individuals weight these differently, so what reads as 'obviously moral' to one person reads as irrelevant or offensive to another.

author: Jonathan Haidt
concept: Groupish and the hive switch: we bind into teams and go blind
summary: Humans are, in Haidt's phrase, 90 percent chimp and 10 percent bee: mostly self-interested but able to flip a hive switch that dissolves the self into a group (a rally, a movement, a team). author: Jonathan Haidt
concept: Morality binds and blinds: moral capital and its cost
summary: Shared moral order (moral capital) is what lets a group trust, cooperate, and sustain itself without constant policing; it is genuinely valuable. But the same binding blinds members to the group's errors and to legitimate outside views. The operator lesson is to value cohesion while deliberately preserving dissent and outside input.
usable_principle: Build enough shared values to bind a group, but engineer in dissent and outside checks so binding does not become blinding.
sniped_relevance: For BJ, a caution as he forms any team or scene: cultivate shared standards (moral capital) but keep a channel for the uncomfortable outside view so the group does not lose contact with reality. source_title: The Coddling of the American Mind
author: Greg Lukianoff and Jonathan Haidt
concept: The three Great Untruths to refuse
summary: Lukianoff and Haidt name three falsehoods that wreck judgment: the Untruth of Fragility (what doesn't kill you makes you weaker), the Untruth of Emotional Reasoning (always trust your feelings), and the Untruth of Us Versus Them (life is a battle between good and evil people). Each is psychologically false and reliably makes people worse off when believed.
usable_principle: Reject the three Untruths: treat hardship as potential growth, distrust raw feeling as fact, and resist sorting people into good vs evil camps.
